response.text:
The Venus of Epicurean philosophy survived in the Virgin of the Schools:

"Donna, sei tanto grande, e tanto vali, / Che qual vuol grazia, e a te non ricorre, / Sua disianza vuol volar senz' ali."

All this was to American thought as though it had never existed. The true American knew the facts but never the feelings; he read the letter, but never felt the law. Before this historical chasm, Adams felt himself helpless; he turned from the Virgin to the Dynamo as though he were a Branly coherer. At the Louvre and at Chartres was the highest energy ever known to man, creator of four-fifths of his noblest art, exercising vastly more attraction over the human mind than all the steam-engines and dynamos ever dreamed of; and yet this energy was unknown to the American mind. An American Virgin would never dare command; an American Venus would never dare exist.

The idea survived only as art. Of American artists who had insisted on the power of sex, as every classic had done, he could think only of Walt Whitman; Bret Harte, as far as the magazines would let him venture; and one or two painters for the flesh-tones. The rest had used sex for sentiment, never for force; to them Eve was a tender flower, and Herodias an unfeminine horror. American art, like the American language and American education, was as far as possible sexless. Society regarded this victory as its greatest triumph, and the historian readily admitted it; he cared nothing for the sex of the dynamo until he could measure its energy.

Vaguely seeking a clue, he stopped almost every day before St. Gaudens's General Sherman in the art exhibit. St. Gaudens himself was in Paris, putting on his usual interminable last touches. Of all the American artists who gave to American art whatever life it breathed in the seventies, he was the most sympathetic but the most inarticulate. The others — the Hunts, Richardson, La Farge, Stanford White — were exuberant; only St. Gaudens could never dilate on an emotion, and could give no form but his own to the creations of his hand.

His health was poor that summer and his spirits low, but Adams risked going to the studio on Mont Parnasse to draw him out for a stroll in the Bois de Boulogne, and in return St. Gaudens sometimes let Adams go about in his company. Once he took him down to Amiens. Not until they were studying the sculpture of the western portal did it dawn on Adams that, for his purposes, St. Gaudens on that spot had more interest than the cathedral itself. Great men before great monuments express great truths, provided they are not taken too solemnly. Adams never tired of quoting Gibbon's supreme phrase before the Gothic cathedrals: "I darted a contemptuous look on the stately monuments of superstition." Gibbon ignored the Virgin because in 1789 religious monuments were out of fashion. One sees what one brings: Gibbon brought the French Revolution; Ruskin brought reaction against it. St. Gaudens had passed beyond all. He loved their dignity, their unity, their scale, their lines and shadows; but he was even less conscious than they of the force that created it all — the Virgin, the Woman — by whose genius "the stately monuments of superstition" were built. The art remained, but the energy was lost even upon the artist.

Yet in mind and person St. Gaudens was a survival of the 1500s; he bore the stamp of the Renaissance, and should have carried an image of the Virgin round his neck like Louis XI. He was a child of Benvenuto Cellini, smothered in an American cradle. Adams was a quintessence of Boston, devoured by curiosity to think like Benvenuto. Each had but half of a nature, and when they came together before the Virgin of Amiens they ought both to have felt in her the force that made them one; but it was not so. To Adams she became more than ever a channel of force; to St. Gaudens she remained as before a channel of taste.

For a symbol of power, St. Gaudens instinctively preferred the horse, as in the Sherman monument. The attitude was so American that for forty years Adams had never realized any other could be in sound taste. Only since 1895 had he begun to feel the Virgin or Venus as force. The idea had died out long ago in the German and English stock. Artists felt a railway train as power, yet constantly complained that the power embodied in a railway train could never be embodied in art. All the steam in the world could not, like the Virgin, build Chartres.

Yet both energies acted as interchangeable force on man, and by action on man all known force may be measured. Symbol or energy, the Virgin had acted as the greatest force the Western world ever felt, and had drawn man's activities to herself more strongly than any other power, natural or supernatural, had ever done; the historian's business was to follow the track of the energy. As a mathematical problem of influence on human progress, all reacted on his mind, and he rather inclined to think the Virgin easiest to handle.

The pursuit was long and tortuous, leading to the vast forests of scholastic science. From Zeno to Descartes, hand in hand with Thomas Aquinas, Montaigne, and Pascal, one stumbled as stupidly as though one were still a German student of 1860. Forty-five years of study had proved quite futile for the pursuit of power; one controlled no more force in 1900 than in 1850, though the amount controlled by society had enormously increased. In such labyrinths the pen becomes a sort of blind-man's dog, and works for itself, modelling the plastic material over and over to the form that suits it best. Compelled once more to lean on this support, Adams covered thousands of pages with figures as formal as algebra, laboriously striking out, altering, burning, experimenting, until the year had expired, the Exposition had long been closed, and winter drawing to its end, before he sailed from Cherbourg, on January 19, 1901, for home.
